hints: Compare the substituents on the two rings, think about what extra electrons the $\text{-OH}$ group has that $\text{-H}$ does not.
Think about what happens when that oxygen lone pair overlaps with the $\pi$ system of the ring, how does electron density in the ring change.
Link increased electron density to the key step in bromination, how easily a $\text{Br}_2$ molecule can be polarised to form $\text{Br}^+$.
walkthrough:
See what the OH group can donate**
Picture phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$. The oxygen has two lone pairs. One of those lone pairs sits in a p-orbital that lines up side by side with the $\pi$ system of the benzene ring. That means those electrons are not stuck on oxygen, they can overlap and spread into the ring. Benzene with just $\text{C-H}$ has nothing extra to donate.

Feel the ring become richer in electrons**
When that lone pair is delocalised into the ring, the total $\pi$ electron density around the ring goes up. You can think of the ring as more negative and more attractive to anything positive. The effect is strongest at the 2, 4 and 6 positions relative to the $\text{OH}$, which is why phenol is 2,4,6 directing.

Connect this to how bromination starts**
Bromination is electrophilic substitution. The $\text{Br-Br}$ molecule must be polarised to $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ ... $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ so that $\text{Br}^+$ can be attacked by the ring. A very electron rich ring like phenol can induce that dipole by itself. Benzene is much less electron rich, so it needs a strong Lewis acid catalyst like $\text{FeBr}_3$ to generate a strong enough electrophile. That is why phenol reacts with $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ instantly at room temperature while benzene does not.

Final answer: The lone pair in a p-orbital on the O atom overlaps / is delocalised into the $\pi$ system of the benzene ring.
This increases $\pi$ electron density in the ring, making the ring more electron rich, especially at the 2, 4 and 6 positions.
The electron rich ring polarises $\text{Br}_2$ more easily, so electrophilic substitution is faster and needs no halogen carrier catalyst.

hints: In $\text{I-Br}$, decide which atom pulls the shared electrons more strongly by comparing the electronegativity of Br and I.
walkthrough:
Let electronegativity decide the electrophile**
In electrophilic substitution the ring always attacks the positive end of the polar molecule. Br is more electronegative than I, so in $\text{I-Br}$ the electrons are pulled toward Br, giving $\text{I}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. With $\text{AlBr}_3$ this generates an iodine centred electrophile, essentially $\text{I}^+$. So iodine bonds to the ring to give iodobenzene, not bromobenzene.
Final answer: Product is iodobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{I}$. Br is more electronegative than I, so the electrophile is $\text{I}^{\delta+}$ / $\text{I}^+$ which attacks the ring.

hints: Treat phenol like an alcohol toward Na, the acidic $\text{O-H}$ gives $\text{H}_2$ and the $\text{-O}^-\text{Na}^+$ salt.
walkthrough:
Write the acid plus metal pattern**
Phenol is acidic enough to react with Na just like an alcohol does. The $\text{O-H}$ breaks, Na replaces H to give sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$, and the released H atoms pair up to $\text{H}_2$. Balance it with 2 phenol to 2 Na to 1 $\text{H}_2$, or use $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$ as shown.

hints: Recall that excess $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ with highly activated phenol substitutes three times, at the positions ortho and para to $\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Place three Br atoms around the OH**
Keep the $\text{-OH}$ where it is and number around the ring. Because the $\text{OH}$ group is so strongly activating, excess bromine puts one Br at each of the two ortho positions (2 and 6) and one at the para position (4). Draw a benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at the top and Br at bottom, bottom left and bottom right. That is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, the white precipitate.
Final answer: R is 2,4,6-tribromophenol: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and Br at positions 2, 4 and 6 relative to $\text{OH}$.

hints: For reaction 1 to give 4-nitrophenol, think about which nitrating mixture is mild enough for the very reactive phenol, not the concentrated acid mix used for benzene.
For reaction 2 to give the $\text{N=N}$ linked product, recall which diazonium electrophile couples with phenol and what pH it needs.
walkthrough:
Choose mild nitration for phenol**
The product in reaction 1 is 4-nitrophenol. Phenol is already so reactive that you must not use the powerful concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ mix at high temperature that benzene needs. Dilute or aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature is enough to give mononitration, mainly para.

Recognise azo coupling conditions**
The product in reaction 2 contains the $\text{-N=N-}$ azo link between two rings. That always comes from coupling of a benzenediazonium ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$, with an activated ring. For phenol the coupling needs alkaline conditions, $\text{NaOH}$ solution, kept cold, to form phenoxide which couples at the para position to give the orange azo dye.

Final answer: reaction 1: dilute / aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$
reaction 2: alkaline / $\text{NaOH}$ and benzenediazonium ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+$ / $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N=N}^+$ as chloride salt)
